newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: France throws wrench into single currency works.
newsitem.headline: France throws wrench into single currency works.

text.p: France threw the European Union's plans for a single currency and its new treaty into turmoil on Monday when it asked for time to study a previously agreed plan to keep budget deficits tight after the currency is launched.

French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn told his EU counterparts at a meeting in Luxembourg that Paris needed time to study the bloc's stability pact, an integral part of its plans for economic and monetary union.
The pact, agreed after hard-fought overnight negotiations in Dublin in December, was supposed to be ratified by EU leaders when they meet in Amsterdam next week.

But Strauss-Kahn, kicking off his debut as finance minister with a bang, said it would take more than a week for Paris to consider the plan, which France wants to be amended with an attachment on employment.
Financial markets initially reacted sharply to the news, with the mark leaping against other European currencies but then settling down.
"It's not the end of EMU in itself, but it's not helping," said Neal Kimberly of Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.
Any hint of an unravelling of the EU's plans for a single currency adds fuel to the belief of some in the market that EMU may have to be delayed from its Jan. 1, 1999 start date.
EU ministers and officials rushed to portray the French move as a momentary blip, a not-unreasonable desire by a new government to look at what its predecessor had accepted.
"There was a great deal of sympathy for the French position," said Dutch Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm, chairman of the meeting.

Strauss-Kahn said France did not want to reopen the agreement on the pact, which could lead to fines on countries running excessive deficits, but he clearly indicated Paris was not happy with the current deal.
"We're not seeking to renegotiate the stability pact, but we cannot approve it today," he told a news conference.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, himself recently at the centre of a storm over plans to revalue German gold reserves to help meet the economic targets for EMU tests, was adamant that the plan not unravel.
"What has been agreed upon and discussed for two years can no longer be put up for negotiation," Waigel told reporters.

France's insistence on an addendum to the pact to spell out how EU countries will coordinate economic policy after the launch of the euro was also seen as threatening the ability of the 15-nation EU to agree on a new treaty at the Amsterdam summit.
Part of the treaty negotiations include discussion of adopting a so-called Employment Chapter to make job creation a formal EU priority. The two were seen as linked by some EU officials.

The French demand for time to consider the stability pact follows a fortnight in which the bloc's plans for the currency have come under intense pressure, in part because of the French election and in part because of Bonn's fiscal difficulties.
Waigel's plan to plug a gaping hole in Bonn's 1997 revenue stream by revaluing the Bundesbank's gold reserves left him politically weakened and accused of trying to cook the books for EMU.
But he remained determined as ever on Monday to argue that governments must bring their 1997 deficits down to 3 percent of gross domestic product -- the EMU target.
